DUET: Decoupled Upper                                                                                             -   and Lower                                         -  Body Execution for
                           Task                  -Agnostic Humanoid Loco                                                                                                -  Manipulation

        Kapalik Khanal, Biswash Khatiwada, Stephen Afrifa, Fan Wu, and Ramesh Bahadur Bist*
          Department of Biological and Agricultural Engineering, North Carolina State University,
                                                                                         Raleigh, North Carolina, USA
                                                                          *Corresponding author:                                           rbbist@ncsu.edu

Abstract                —       Changing    a    humanoid    robot's    manipulation    policy    should    not    require    retraining    the
controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution
framework       that       enables       locomotion       and       manipulation       controllers       to       operate       sim                                                                                        ultaneously       by
combining          their          commands          only          at          the          robot          interface.          A          reinforcement                                                    -learning          locomotion
policy  controls  the  12  leg  joints  and  a  waist  yaw  joint,  tracking  planar  velocity,  turning  rate,  and
pelvis height from deep crouching to upright stand                                                                                   ing on a 23                  -degree             -of     -freedom Unitree G1. The
10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included
only  as  observations,  so  that  any  compatible  manipulation  policy  that  generates  arm                                                                                                                                   -joint  targets
can         control              the         upper         body,         and         the         locomotion         policy         keeps         the         lower         body         stable         without
requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on
hardware    by    pairing    the    same    locomotion    checkpoint    with    two    different    vision                                                                                                            -lan       guage           -action
models,         GR00T         N1.7         and         pi0.5.         In         simulation         evaluation,         the         locomotion         controller         kept         the
robot's   lower   body   stable   with   no   falls   while   tracking   the   commanded   planar   velocity,   yaw   rate,
and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s,                                                                                        and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies
identify   the                  upper   body                    pose   curriculum   as   the   dominant   component,   and   removing   this   training
step       reduces       episode       survival       from       20.0       to       7.4       seconds       and       increases       the       fall       rate       to       6.06       per
environment       minute.       Robustness       tests       show       no       falls       under       pushes       of       up       to       1.0       m/s       within       th                                                                            e
trained     payload     range,     and     no     falls     at     twice     the     payload     limit     for     pushes     below     0.7     m/s.     These
results            show            that            a            manipulation            policy            can            be            exchanged            without            retraining,            restarting,            or
otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot                                                                                  upright.
Keywords                  —      Humanoid          robots,          legged          locomotion,          reinforcement          learning,          loco                                                                     -manipulation,
vision         -language                  -action models.

I. INTRODUCTION
Humanoid robots are increasingly expected to perform manipulation while remaining mobile. Yet
locomotion   and   manipulation   are   often   developed   under   different   objectives   and   later   integrated
into   a   single   robotic   system   [1].   Locomotion   controllers   typically                                                                                               optimize                  for      dynamic   stability
under prescribed body motions, whereas manipulation policies are trained to generate task                                                                                                                                                   -specific
upper          -body behaviors [1], [2]. Combining the two                                                                          control components                                   often requires joint training,
whole           -body          policy          design,          or          explicit          coordination          between          controllers,          making          the          resulting
system               difficult               to               modify               when               the               manipulation               task               or               policy               changes.               Although               such
approaches        can        produce        coordinated        behavior,                                                        they        can        also        create        dependencies        between        the
manipulation policy and the controller responsible for maintaining balance. As a result, changing
the      manipulation      behavior      may      require      modification,      adaptation,      or      retraining      elsewhere      in      the
control stack.
A    more    modular    alternative    is    to    treat    lower                                                       -body    stabilization    as    a    reusable    capability    that    can
remain   unchanged   while   independently   developed   manipulation   policies   control   the   upper   body.
